passage: Class teacher's note. Yesterday in the corridor I watched Seema walk past while two boys blocked Jomon's way and took his cap. She did not look at him and kept her eyes on her water bottle. When I asked her about it later, she shrugged and said, "Not my problem." I said I was not scolding, only asking. She was quiet for a while and then said that everybody else had walked by too. I asked if she would like to help next time, and she said she would think about it. I have spoken with Jomon and the two boys. I will check in with Seema on Friday and ask her and Jomon to help me set up the library shelves.

qa.q: What did Seema say when the teacher asked her about it?
qa.a: She shrugged and said, "Not my problem."

qa.q: What does Seema's staring at her water bottle suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uncomfortable and wanted to avoid getting involved, telling herself it was not her problem, though the teacher cannot be certain.

qa.q: What could Seema do next time she sees a child being blocked and taunted?
qa.a: She could tell an adult, stay near the child or ask if they are okay, so nobody is left alone just because everyone assumes someone else will help.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt as people walked past?
qa.a: Jomon was probably lonely and hurt as people walked by without helping.

grounding: A teacher's note about a child who tells herself it is not her problem and turns away from someone being bullied.

passage:
In the school canteen, Vinita saw two boys pour salt into Suraj's juice while he fetched a spoon. They sniggered. Suraj came back, took a sip and spat it out, red-faced.
Vinita turned back to her sandwich. Not my problem, she told herself. Someone else will say something.
But nobody did. Everyone was busy. Suraj sat alone, staring at his cup.
Vinita chewed slowly. The sandwich felt like cardboard. If everyone waits for someone else, then no one helps.
She got up and bought Suraj a fresh juice. "Here. I saw what they did." Then she told the canteen supervisor, who went to talk to the two boys.

qa.q: What did the boys pour into Suraj's juice?
What was Vinita feeling as she chewed her sandwich?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and guilty; the sandwich felt like cardboard as she realised no one was helping.

qa.q: What did Vinita do to become the one who helps?
qa.a: She bought Suraj a fresh juice, told him she had seen it, and reported it to the canteen supervisor.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel sitting alone before Vinita came?
qa.a: Suraj probably felt humiliated and alone, staring at his cup while no one seemed to care.

grounding: A girl tells herself a prank is not her problem and turns away, then realises everyone is waiting for someone else and becomes the one who helps.

passage:
Monday. At the bus stop, older kids flicked Sunaina's ponytail and called her "horse". Bhupen put his earphones in. Not my business, he thought.
Tuesday. It happened again. Sunaina stood very still, looking at the road. Other kids looked away too. Bhupen noticed: everyone was waiting for someone else.
Wednesday. When the older kids started, Bhupen took out his earphones and walked over to stand beside Sunaina. "Hey. Want to see the comic I got?" The older kids muttered and moved off.
That evening he told his mother, who phoned the school transport in-charge.

qa.q: What did the older kids call Sunaina?
What was Bhupen thinking on Monday?
qa.a: He felt it wasn't his business and turned away, choosing the comfort of not caring.

qa.q: What changed Bhupen's choice on Wednesday?
qa.a: He noticed everyone was waiting for someone else to help, so he became the one who stood beside Sunaina and later told his mother.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Bhupen comes to stand beside her?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel less alone and relieved when the older kids move off.

grounding: A boy tells himself bullying at the bus stop is not his business, then notices everyone is waiting for someone else and becomes the one who helps.
